analysis.one_liner: Shields computer and software makers from most Y2K lawsuits and waives antitrust rules for Y2K fixes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 9 cosponsors in July 1998, never got a committee hearing or a House vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: As the year-2000 date problem loomed, this bill would have rewritten the rules for lawsuits over computer failures tied to the date change. Most Y2K suits would be treated as contract claims, with money recovery limited to business losses and repair or replacement costs, and companies that gave notice and offered fixes would be largely shielded. It would also have suspended antitrust rules for companies cooperating on Y2K repairs through the end of 2001.
analysis.who_benefits: Software and computer makers, and any business facing Y2K lawsuits, would gain the most. Suits over computer date failures would be reclassified as contract claims, barring theories like negligence and the larger damages that come with them, and recovery would be capped at business losses and repair or replacement costs — and only for defendants who gave notice and offered fixes. Competitors would also be free to work together on Y2K fixes without antitrust exposure through 2001.

how_it_helps.text: For companies facing Y2K lawsuits, the bill would have converted most suits into contract claims, which generally allow smaller recoveries and exclude punitive damages, cutting their litigation exposure.

Sellers that gave notice and offered free repairs or replacements for products sold after 1994 would be largely shielded from suit, giving them a financial incentive to fix Y2K problems rather than fight lawsuits.

The antitrust exemption would have let rival companies share information and coordinate on Y2K fixes without fear of price-fixing or collusion claims, with a carve-out keeping outright boycotts illegal.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone harmed by a Y2K computer failure — businesses and consumers — would bear more of their own losses, because lawsuits would be treated as contract claims with recovery limited to business losses and repair or replacement costs. Shareholders suing over failures to detect or disclose Y2K problems would face the same limits, and state antitrust enforcement would be suspended for Y2K-related cooperation through the end of 2001.

drawbacks.text: Buyers of defective computers and software would have absorbed more of their own losses: the bill capped recovery at business losses and repair costs and excluded emotional harm, shifting the cost of products that failed from sellers to customers.

The bill would have covered shareholder and derivative suits over failures to detect, disclose, or fix Y2K problems, limiting investors' ability to recover from companies that misled them about their Y2K readiness.

The antitrust exemption ran through December 31, 2001 and covered any conduct 'solely' aimed at Y2K mitigation, a broad window in which competitors could coordinate with limited enforcement beyond a narrow boycott exception.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest case for the bill was that fear of lawsuits might discourage companies from disclosing and fixing Y2K problems, and the free-repair conditions did tie the shield to actual remediation. But the trade was lopsided: it stripped negligence and securities-fraud remedies from nearly every potential Y2K plaintiff, left customers and shareholders carrying losses caused by defective products, and opened a three-year antitrust safe harbor defined mainly by the companies' own say-so. For ordinary computer owners, the costs outweighed the promised speedup in fixes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in July 1998 and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Dreier introduced the bill on July 16, 1998, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
The committee held no hearings, took no vote, and never reported the bill; the last entry in its action history is a referral note pointing readers to the Senate companion bill, S. 2392.
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Computer buyers, businesses, and shareholders kept their full legal remedies for Y2K failures, since the liability limits never took effect. The software and computer industry went on facing ordinary litigation risk.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; of the bill's nine cosponsors, eight were Republicans and one was a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would have given the industry the liability cap it sought: suits over Y2K failures would become contract claims with recovery limited to business losses and repair costs, so companies that shipped non-compliant products would pay less for the harm they caused. The shield was conditioned on offering notice and free repairs to buyers.

The bill would have sharply narrowed the claims plaintiffs' lawyers could bring over Y2K failures, since contract-only treatment forecloses negligence and other tort theories and their larger recoveries. On this bill, the plaintiffs' bar's interest in full lawsuits ran alongside injured computer owners' interests.

Capping recovery at business losses and repair costs would have reduced the payouts liability insurers and their policyholders faced from Y2K claims. The savings would come at the expense of the people and businesses those claims were meant to compensate.
